name: Learn: Configuration & Security
objective: CKAD › Application Environment, Configuration & Security (25%). Goal: wire ConfigMaps and Secrets into a container as env vars and volumes, set resource requests/limits, lock a container down with a securityContext (non-root, dropped capabilities), and run a Pod under a dedicated ServiceAccount — the configuration-and-security tasks the exam leans on.
description: Master the CKAD configuration and security domain step by step — inject ConfigMaps and Secrets into pods (env and volumes), constrain containers with resource requests/limits, harden them with a securityContext, and bind a pod to a purpose-built ServiceAccount. Everything is plain object-level kubectl.

questions.title: ConfigMap as env vars (configMapKeyRef + envFrom)
questions.teach:
A **ConfigMap** holds non-secret config as key/value pairs so you don't bake settings into the image. A container can consume it **three** ways — know all of them, the exam mixes them:
- **One key → one env var** with `env[].valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` (name + key) — rename or cherry-pick a single value.
- **Every key → env vars of the same name** with `envFrom.configMapRef` — bulk-import the whole ConfigMap. Add a `prefix:` to namespace the vars if you like.
- **As a volume** with `volumes[].configMap` + a `volumeMount` — **each key becomes a file** in the mount path (ideal for config files like nginx.conf). Use `items` to project only chosen keys to specific paths, and `subPath` on the mount to drop a single file into a directory **without hiding the rest of it**.

**Gotchas the exam leans on:**
- Env values (`env`/`envFrom`) are read **once at pod start** — editing the ConfigMap won't update a running pod's env. **Mounted volume keys DO update** live (eventual, cache-delayed), *unless* you used `subPath`, which freezes that file.
- A referenced ConfigMap/key must exist at pod start or the pod won't start — mark a key `optional: true` to tolerate it being absent.
- `kubectl create configmap` sources: `--from-literal=k=v`, `--from-file=file` (filename→key), `--from-file=key=file` (rename), `--from-env-file=f` (whole file of k=v pairs).
- `immutable: true` locks a ConfigMap so it can't be changed (only deleted/recreated) — protects against accidental edits and reduces apiserver load.
- Symmetry to remember: everything here applies to **Secrets** too — just swap `configMap*` → `secret*`.
questions.prompt:
Namespace `ckad-config` already has a ConfigMap `app-cfg` with keys `APP_COLOR=blue` and `APP_MODE=prod`. Create a pod `cfg-pod` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) that:
- sets env var `COLOR` from the `APP_COLOR` key via `configMapKeyRef`, and
- imports the whole `app-cfg` ConfigMap via `envFrom` (so `APP_MODE` appears as-is).

Target: inside the pod, `COLOR=blue` and `APP_MODE=prod`.
questions.hint: Start from `kubectl run cfg-pod --image=busybox:1.36 -n ckad-config --dry-run=client -o yaml -- sh -c 'sleep 3600' > p.yaml`, then under the container add `env:` with a `valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` (name: app-cfg, key: APP_COLOR) for `COLOR`, plus `envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: app-cfg}}]`. Apply it.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cfg-pod
  namespace: ckad-config
spec:
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - name: COLOR
      valueFrom:
        configMapKeyRef:
          name: app-cfg
          key: APP_COLOR
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: app-cfg
EOF
kubectl -n ckad-config exec cfg-pod -- env | grep -E 'COLOR|APP_MODE'

questions.title: Secret as env var and as a mounted volume
questions.teach:
A **Secret** is like a ConfigMap but for sensitive data. Note: it is **base64-encoded, NOT encrypted** at rest by default (anyone with `get secret` + base64 can read it) — encryption at rest is a separate cluster feature. It supports the **same three** methods — the symmetry is worth memorizing, because the exam expects a Secret to do everything a ConfigMap does:
- **One key → one env var** via `env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef` — but the value is then visible in `env`/process listings.
- **Every key → env vars** via `envFrom.secretRef` — the bulk-import, exactly like `envFrom.configMapRef`.
- **As a volume** via `volumes[].secret.secretName` + a `volumeMount` — each key becomes a file (preferred for TLS certs/tokens); use `items` to project selected keys and `defaultMode` to set file perms (e.g. `0400`).

**Gotchas the exam leans on:**
- Anything a ConfigMap does (single-key, `envFrom`, volume, `items`/`subPath`, `optional: true`, `immutable: true`), a Secret does — just swap `configMap*` → `secret*`.
- Volume-mounted Secrets **update live**; env-injected ones are **frozen at pod start** (and `subPath` freezes a mounted file too).
- **Secret types** matter: `generic`/`Opaque` (arbitrary k/v), `kubernetes.io/tls` (needs `tls.crt`+`tls.key`, used by Ingress), `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` (image-pull creds, referenced via `imagePullSecrets`), `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`.
- Create with `kubectl create secret generic s --from-literal=k=v` / `--from-file=...`; `kubectl create secret tls`; `kubectl create secret docker-registry`. In YAML, `data:` holds base64 values while `stringData:` lets you write plaintext (kubelet encodes it).
questions.prompt:
Namespace `ckad-config` has a Secret `db-cred` with keys `DB_USER=admin` and `DB_PASS=s3cr3t`. Create a pod `sec-pod` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) that:
- sets env var `DB_PASS` from the secret's `DB_PASS` key via `secretKeyRef`, and
- mounts the whole `db-cred` Secret as a volume at `/etc/creds` (read-only is fine).

Target: env `DB_PASS=s3cr3t`, and file `/etc/creds/DB_USER` contains `admin`.
questions.hint: Add under the container `env:` with `valueFrom.secretKeyRef` (name: db-cred, key: DB_PASS), a `volumeMounts` entry (name: creds, mountPath: /etc/creds), and a pod-level `volumes:` entry `secret: {secretName: db-cred}`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sec-pod
  namespace: ckad-config
spec:
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - name: DB_PASS
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-cred
          key: DB_PASS
    volumeMounts:
    - name: creds
      mountPath: /etc/creds
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: creds
    secret:
      secretName: db-cred
EOF
kubectl -n ckad-config exec sec-pod -- sh -c 'echo $DB_PASS; cat /etc/creds/DB_USER'

questions.title: Resource requests and limits
questions.teach:
**Requests** tell the scheduler how much CPU/memory a container needs (used to pick a node and reserve capacity). **Limits** cap how much it may use. Set them under `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` on the **container** (each container is budgeted separately; the pod's total is the sum).

**Units:** CPU in cores or **millicores** (`250m` = 0.25 core). Memory in bytes with power-of-two suffixes `Ki`/`Mi`/`Gi` or decimal `K`/`M`/`G` — `128Mi` ≠ `128M`. Watch the capitalization.

**Gotchas the exam leans on:**
- **Memory over the limit → container is OOM-killed** (and restarted per `restartPolicy`). **CPU over the limit → throttled, never killed.** This distinction is a favorite question.
- **QoS classes** derive from requests/limits: `Guaranteed` (every container has limits == requests for both cpu+mem), `Burstable` (at least a request set), `BestEffort` (none set). QoS drives eviction order under node pressure (BestEffort evicted first).
- Omitting a request but setting a limit makes the request **default to the limit**. A limit with no request still works.
- A **LimitRange** in the namespace can inject defaults or enforce min/max; a **ResourceQuota** can require every pod to declare requests/limits and cap the namespace total — a pod missing them may be rejected.
- Other resources use the same block, e.g. `requests`/`limits` for `ephemeral-storage` and extended resources like `nvidia.com/gpu` (GPUs must be set in **limits**).
questions.prompt:
Create a pod `res-pod` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) in `ckad-config` with the container's resources set to:
- requests: `cpu=100m`, `memory=64Mi`
- limits: `cpu=250m`, `memory=128Mi`

Target: the container shows exactly those requests and limits.
questions.hint: `kubectl run res-pod --image=busybox:1.36 -n ckad-config --restart=Never -o yaml --dry-run=client -- sh -c 'sleep 3600' > r.yaml`, then add a `resources:` block. Or use `--requests`/`--limits`... those flags are deprecated, so prefer editing YAML.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: res-pod
  namespace: ckad-config
spec:
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 64Mi
      limits:
        cpu: 250m
        memory: 128Mi
EOF
kubectl -n ckad-config get pod res-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'

verification.description: res-pod container has requests 100m/64Mi and limits 250m/128Mi

questions.title: Container securityContext: non-root + drop ALL capabilities
questions.teach:
A **securityContext** hardens how a container runs. It exists at **two levels** — pod-level (`spec.securityContext`) and container-level (`spec.containers[].securityContext`). For overlapping fields the **container-level value wins**; but some fields live at only one level.

**Container-level only:**
- `runAsNonRoot: true` — kubelet refuses to start the container if the image would run as UID 0.
- `runAsUser` / `runAsGroup` — force a specific UID/GID.
- `capabilities.add` / `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` — add/strip Linux capabilities; dropping ALL is the least-privilege default (capabilities are **container-only**).
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` — makes `/` immutable; the app then needs a **writable `emptyDir`** mounted at any path it writes (e.g. `/tmp`, logs) or it will error.
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` — blocks gaining more privs than the parent (setuid binaries, etc.).
- `privileged: true` — full host access; the opposite of hardening.

**Pod-level (can also sit at container level where noted):**
- `fsGroup` — group that owns mounted volumes (so a non-root UID can write to them).
- `runAsUser`/`runAsGroup`/`runAsNonRoot` — act as defaults inherited by containers.
- `seccompProfile.type` — `RuntimeDefault`, `Localhost`, or `Unconfined`.

**Gotchas the exam leans on:**
- `runAsNonRoot: true` only **verifies** the UID isn't 0 at startup — it does NOT pick a UID. Pair it with `runAsUser: <non-zero>`, or the image must already declare a non-root user, else `CreateContainerConfigError`.
- `capabilities` and `readOnlyRootFilesystem` **cannot** be set at pod level — container only.
- Dropping `ALL` then re-adding one (e.g. `add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]`) is the clean way to bind low ports as non-root.
questions.prompt:
Create a pod `sctx-pod` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) in `ckad-config` whose container's `securityContext` has `runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 1000`, and drops `ALL` capabilities.

Target: inside the pod, `id -u` prints `1000`, and the spec shows capabilities.drop includes ALL.
questions.hint: Under the container add `securityContext:` with `runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 1000`, and `capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}`. busybox runs fine as a non-root UID.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sctx-pod
  namespace: ckad-config
spec:
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
EOF
kubectl -n ckad-config exec sctx-pod -- id -u   # -> 1000

verification.description: sctx-pod runs as UID 1000 (non-root) with ALL capabilities dropped

questions.title: ServiceAccount: run a pod under it, no token auto-mount
questions.teach:
Every pod runs as a **ServiceAccount** (the namespace's `default` SA unless you set `spec.serviceAccountName`). Giving a workload its own SA lets you grant it exactly the RBAC it needs — least privilege. Create one with `kubectl create sa app-sa -n <ns>`.

By default Kubernetes auto-mounts the SA's API token into the pod at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount` (files `token`, `ca.crt`, `namespace`). If the workload never calls the API, set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` to avoid handing it a credential it doesn't need.

**Gotchas the exam leans on:**
- `automountServiceAccountToken` can be set on the **SA** (applies to all its pods) **or** on the **pod spec** — the **pod-level value wins** when both are present.
- The SA only grants permissions once you bind it with RBAC: a **RoleBinding** (namespaced) or **ClusterRoleBinding**, with `subjects: [{kind: ServiceAccount, name: ..., namespace: ...}]`. An SA with no binding can still authenticate but is authorized for nothing.
- The mounted token is a **projected volume** (`serviceAccountToken`): short-lived, auto-rotated, audience-bound. Since 1.24 `kubectl create sa` no longer auto-creates a long-lived Secret token — generate one on demand with `kubectl create token <sa>`, or create a `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` Secret manually if you need a static one.
- Reference image-pull credentials from an SA via its `imagePullSecrets` so every pod using it inherits them.
- `serviceAccount` (deprecated alias) vs `serviceAccountName` — use `serviceAccountName`.
questions.prompt:
In `ckad-config`, create a ServiceAccount `app-sa`, then create a pod `sa-pod` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) that runs under `app-sa` with `automountServiceAccountToken: false`.

Target: `sa-pod`'s `serviceAccountName` is `app-sa`, and no SA token is mounted inside the pod.
questions.hint: `kubectl create sa app-sa -n ckad-config`. Then in the pod spec set `serviceAccountName: app-sa` and `automountServiceAccountToken: false` (both at the pod spec level).
questions.solution:
kubectl create sa app-sa -n ckad-config
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sa-pod
  namespace: ckad-config
spec:
  serviceAccountName: app-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
EOF
kubectl -n ckad-config exec sa-pod -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount 2>&1 || echo 'no token (expected)'

verification.description: sa-pod runs as SA app-sa with the API token NOT auto-mounted
